title: Ramah Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Ramah wells have a 264-foot median depth, 10 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $19,200-$30,400.
h1: Ramah, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost Guide
intro_html:
For rural property around Ramah, the nearby well records show a wide spread in drilling conditions. The median completed well is 264 feet deep, but the middle half runs from 70 to 400 feet. Reported yields are stronger than many buyers expect, with a 10.0 gallon-per-minute median among wells that list a pump yield.

These records cover permitted wells within 5 miles of Ramah in El Paso County. They are useful for planning, but they do not guarantee what a new well will find on one specific lot. Check nearby permits, aquifer information, water rights, septic requirements, and access before buying or bidding a build.

sections.heading: Ramah well depths vary across the Denver Basin
sections.html:
Depth is the first major cost variable around Ramah. The median recorded depth is 264 feet, while the middle half of wells falls between 70 and 400 feet. The 90th percentile is 529 feet, and the deepest well on record reaches 780 feet.

The depth mix shows why a single neighboring well is not enough for a bid: 32% are under 100 feet, 23% are between 100 and 300 feet, 37% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 8% exceed 600 feet. Permits identify Denver Basin aquifer wells throughout this area, including Arapahoe, Quaternary Alluvium, and unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. Sedimentary bedrock and local aquifer conditions can move the drilling target substantially.

sections.heading: What Ramah wells produce for household use
sections.html:
Among the 223 wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 7.0 to 14.0 gallons per minute. Most reported wells fall in the 5-to-15-gpm range, which accounts for 61% of the records, while 25% report more than 15 gpm.

No reported well in this set is under 1 gpm. Still, 14% fall between 1 and 5 gpm, so a buyer should not assume every parcel will match the median. A domestic well also has a legal pumping limit tied to its permit; an exempt household-use well is generally limited to 35 gpm. Larger irrigation or expanded uses may require different water-right planning.

sections.heading: Static water levels and the local record
sections.html:
Only 38 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is much smaller than the depth and yield samples. The median depth to water is 199 feet, with the middle half between 93 and 249 feet below the surface.

Measurements from the 2010s show a 210-foot median water level, compared with 182 feet in the 2020s. That change does not show a dropping water table in these records; the later median is shallower. It also is not a complete groundwater trend because the number of measurements is limited and the wells may not be comparable. Ask for the well-specific static level, pumping level, and construction report rather than relying only on the area median.

sections.heading: Ramah permit history and the drillers on record
sections.html:
Ramah has a long permit history, with records dating back to the 1950s and a newest permit year of 2025. The largest permit period was the 1990s, with 127 permits. The records show 96 permits in the 2000s, 74 in the 2010s, and 46 in the 2020s.

For older local work, the most active driller in the records is Hamacher Well Works Inc, also listed as Hamacher, Alan Ray, with 241 wells. Can America Drilling, Inc., also listed as Arde, Wayne A., appears on 41. Kunau Drilling Llc, listed as Kunau, Timothy R., appears on 25. These names help trace local construction history, but they are not a guarantee of availability, price, or performance on a new project.

sections.heading: Ramah well drilling cost at the median depth
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot for Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 264-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $13,200 to $18,400.

A finished well, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, is estimated at $19,200 to $30,400 at that median depth. A quote can move outside that range if the well is substantially deeper, access is difficult, casing or grout requirements change, or the site needs more trenching and electrical work. Get the driller to state what depth is included, what happens if the hole is dry or low-yield, and which completion items are included.

sections.heading: Checks before buying or building near Ramah
sections.html:
Water quality deserves its own review. Mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not establish contamination in a particular well, but it is a reason to test existing water and ask for location-specific sampling information before closing.

Review the well construction report, permit conditions, yield test, static water level, casing and grout, and the distance to the proposed septic system. Confirm that the parcel can support the intended household, stock, or irrigation use. Colorado DWR records show domestic or household use on 55% of the records, stock use on 53%, irrigation on 7%, and monitoring on 6%, so the permit's actual use matters.

For a new build, verify access for a rig, space for equipment, a legal septic layout, electrical routing, and a plan if the first hole is dry or produces less than expected.

sections.heading: A practical Ramah lot-buying plan
sections.html:
Start with the closest permitted wells, not a countywide average. Compare their depths, named aquifers, reported yields, static levels, construction details, and permit uses. Nearby Simla, Calhan, Matheson, Peyton, Elbert, and Yoder can provide broader context, but conditions can change across short distances, so Ramah-area records should carry the most weight for a Ramah parcel.

For an existing home, make the sale contingent on reviewing the permit and testing the water. For vacant land, obtain a driller's site-specific estimate and ask how the quote handles extra depth, low yield, and completion work. A well that makes 10.0 gpm may be comfortable for a typical household, but the permit, storage system, septic design, and intended use still control what the property can support.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Ramah, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth near Ramah is 264 feet. The middle half runs from 70 to 400 feet, while the 90th percentile is 529 feet and the deepest record is 780 feet. That spread matters for budgeting: a nearby shallow well does not establish the depth a new well will need on your lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Ramah?
faq.a: At the 264-foot median depth, the estimated drilled-hole cost is $13,200 to $18,400 using a $50-to-$70-per-foot rate. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $19,200 to $30,400. A deeper hole, difficult access, or added completion work can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Ramah, Colorado?
faq.a: Among 223 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 7.0 to 14.0 gpm. Sixty-one percent report 5 to 15 gpm, and 25% report more than 15 gpm. Fourteen percent are between 1 and 5 gpm, so site-specific results still matter.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Ramah?
faq.a: The records do not establish that every Ramah well is safe for drinking. Within about 10 miles, mapped environmental information includes 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the actual well water, review its construction and location, and use current laboratory results before relying on it for household use.

faq.q: What should I check before buying land with a well near Ramah?
faq.a: Review the DWR permit, construction report, yield test, static water level, aquifer, casing, grout, and permitted use. The local median static water level is 199 feet below the surface, but only 38 records report one. Also confirm septic setbacks, access for a drilling rig, electrical needs, and what happens if a new hole is low-yield or dry.
